newsitem.title: USA: Sudan hostage deal said not at odds with U.S. policy.
newsitem.headline: Sudan hostage deal said not at odds with U.S. policy.

text.p: The United States said on Monday a U.S. congressmen's intervention in freeing three Red Cross workers held hostage by Sudanese rebels did not reverse U.S. policy against negotiating with or rewarding terrorists.

The three aid workers -- an American, an Australian and a Kenyan -- were released after Democratic Representative Bill Richardson of New Mexico, an American ambassador and a Sudanese diplomat teamed up to persuade the rebels to drop a demand for millions of dollars in ransom.
Instead, the rebels settled for promises of five tons of rice, four Jeeps, nine radios and a health survey for their disease-ridden camp.
"Certainly, we supported him in his efforts," State Department deputy spokesman Glyn Davies said of Richardson's mission.
"The policy of the United States is that we don't pay ransom, that we don't encourage others to pay ransom," he said.

"But we're not going to stand in the way of third parties if they see fit to reach some accommodation with those holding their employees or, indeed, to stand in the way of family members who wish to negotiate with captors of their families," Davies added.
The spokesman said the International Committee of the Red Cross, not the United States, paid for the rice and equipment.

He insisted this was a "private deal ... not a deal on behalf the people of the United States by the government of the United States" even though Richardson is a congressmen, has close ties to President Bill Clinton, has undertaken other missions with tacit White House approval and was accompanied by the U.S. ambassador to Sudan, Timothy Carney.
Also instrumental in the negotiation effort was the Sudanese ambassador to the United States, Mahdi I. Mohamed.
Asked if the deal might encourage other potential hostage-takers, Davies said: "We certainly hope not."

American pilot John Early, Australian nurse Maree Worthington and Kenyan pilot Mohsin Raza flew out of the Sudanese bush to Geneva on board a U.S. military plane on Monday to a welcome with flowers and cameras.

The three fell into the hands of militia led by Commander Kerubino Kwanyin Kol on Nov. 1 when their plane landed at Wunrok in southern Sudan to take home five Sudanese soldier patients discharged from a Red Cross hospital in Kenya.
The rebels, a breakaway group of the rebel Sudan People's Liberation Army (SPLA), accused the ICRC of providing assistance to the mainstream SPLA. Early's family asked for Richardson's intervention.
The militia is still holding the patients from the plane and the Red Cross said it would do everything possible to ensure they can return to their homes, which are in the area.

The SPLA has been fighting for autonomy of the mainly Christian and animist south against Khartoum's Moslem government for 13 years. Most of the victims have been civilians displaced from their homes or reduced to starvation.
In 1993, Washington put Sudan, Africa's largest and one of its poorest nations on its list of states accused of sponsoring terrorism.

Sudanese leaders and diplomats have been accused by the United States of taking part in conspiracies to blow up landmarks and tunnels in New York, to assassinate President Hosni Mubakar of Egypt and to provide safe harbour for international terrorists. The U.S. Embassay in the capital Khartoum was closed in February after the Central Intelligence Agency warned of a threat to embasdsy workers.
